articleTitle: Spend to save measures: their financial justification
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Life Cycle Costing and the Business Plan
abstract: A decade or so ago, interest in life cycle costs was revived by the realisation that, for many types of equipment, in-service costs could be many times acquisition cost. Expectation of reducing the former now motivates much work towards improved reliability, maintainability and logistics. In consequence, proposals are often made for 'spend to save' measures in which extra initial expenditure is shown to result subsequently in large net savings as the benefits of reduced running costs accumulate over the years. However, these proposals frequently receive less than enthusiastic receptions from those who hold the purse strings. Their constant call may be for savings; but when proffered specific opportunities for these they then seem to adopt an inconsistent attitude-appearing to have concern only for initial expenditures when disregarding much greater subsequent benefits. This paper reviews common difficulties in the way of financial justification of spend to save measures, analyses them and suggests how they may best be overcome.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Life Cycle Costing and the Business Plan
abstract: Many British companies have been showing a growing interest in improving their project management performance. In particular they have been wanting to increase the likeliho od of completing their projects to predetermined time and cost targets. This has been necessary because over the last decade a wide range of industries has witnessed significant changes in customer attitude and expectations. Principally these changes are the replacement of cost plus by fixed price contracting, narrower profit margins and increasing competition. To meet these demanding requirements an increasing number of these organisations have adopted integrated cost and schedule control (C/SC) to assist in the achievement of these project management improvements. This paper outlines a recommended process for establishing and maintaining cost and schedule control of a project through the use of an earned value based performance measurement system.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Life cycle costs of aircraft systems
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Life Cycle Costing and the Business Plan
abstract: For some time the Ministry of Defence (MoD) has been placing an increasing emphasis on life cycle costs (LCC) to ensure they are given proper weight in procurement decisions. It is only by looking at the life cycle costs that one can be certain that the apparent attractiveness of cheaper acquisition options is not outweighed by later high in-service costs. This paper examines the major elements of aircraft system LCC and highlights some of the complexities involved. The emphasis is on aircraft but the principles apply equally to sea and land systems.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Condition monitoring and its contribution to life cycle costs
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Life Cycle Costing and the Business Plan
abstract: Condition monitoring as part of a predictive maintenance program can dramatically reduce machine operating costs, as well as extending the life of machines. The ways that this is achieved are diverse and different in almost every operation. However, almost any one of them allows justification of the costs involved, with the result that when all returns are added together, the potential returns are considerable.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Life Cycle Costing and the Business Plan
abstract: Predicting how much an activity costs and when these costs will occur is of fundamental importance to assessing the feasibility of a project. Furthermore if it is decided to proceed with a project these estimates can be used to generate the budget for the project, to ascertain what a fair price would be if the work was to be undertaken by a contractor, as an indirect indicator of the quality of bought goods, materials and services and as a tool in the cost and time control in project management. Early on in projects many assumptions will be needed on the characteristics of the project itself and on how external influences will affect the feasibility of the project, such as Government policy, currency exchange rates and inflation. It is important to record such assumptions formally and in detail so that at later stages it can be seen readily what amendments need to be made to any previous forecasts. The author discusses top down and bottom up methods of estimation and then discusses objective estimates, subjective estimates, comparative estimates, synthetic estimates and parametric estimates.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Life Cycle Costing and the Business Plan
abstract: The author describes the use of spreadsheet packages (Lotus 1-2-3 in this case) in general for the development of short-term and long-term plans. The author also describes the application of a model developed for evaluating investments in waste recycling plants.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>
